title: Building DevERP: Designing an Offline-First Desktop ERP with SQLite WAL Mode
snippet: Why we chose SQLite over cloud databases for software consultant cash flow tracking, and how PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL eliminates lock contention.
htmlContent:
Software consultants and freelance engineers frequently handle sensitive multi-currency bank wires, deliverables, and invoices across varying internet reliability. When engineering DevERP PRO, we chose an unapologetically offline-first philosophy: 100% data sovereignty, zero cloud database dependencies, and sub-millisecond local queries.

The Problem with Traditional Desktop Database Locking

By default, SQLite uses a rollback journal for atomic commits. This operates by acquiring an exclusive lock on the database file whenever a write occurs. On a Windows desktop with active WPF UI data binding, running a background batch import or generating a 30-day runway cash flow report while simultaneously creating an invoice caused visible 200–500ms dispatcher stutters.

The Solution: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

In WAL mode, changes are written to a separate .db-wal file rather than overwriting the original database file. Readers never wait for writers, and writers never wait for readers.

// DevErpDbContext.cs - SQLite Initialization
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder optionsBuilder)
{
    var connection = new SqliteConnection(connectionString);
    connection.Open();

    using var command = connection.CreateCommand();
    command.CommandText = @"
        PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
        PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
        PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;
        PRAGMA mmap_size = 268435456;
    ";
    command.ExecuteNonQuery();
    optionsBuilder.UseSqlite(connection);
}

Key Production Takeaways

  • Concurrent Read/Write: Financial forecasting calculations run in the background without freezing user input in WPF.
  • Instant Crash Recovery: If the desktop app terminates abruptly during a power outage, the uncommitted WAL transactions rollback cleanly on next launch.
  • Portability: A complete encrypted snapshot of the user's business can be exported as a single file and restored anywhere in seconds.

title: EF Core Query Optimization: Taming N+1 Queries and Split Queries in Production
snippet: How Cartesian explosions occur with multi-level includes, and how AsSplitQuery() combined with lean projection DTOs drops latency by 70%.
htmlContent:
Entity Framework Core is the gold standard ORM in the .NET ecosystem, but naïve usage can degrade database throughput. When profiling e-commerce endpoints in Tech Xpress, two common query antipatterns emerged: Cartesian multiplication and accidental entity tracking.

1. The Cartesian Explosion Problem

When you write an eager loading query with multiple collections, EF Core executes a single SQL query with multiple LEFT JOIN clauses, duplicating header columns across dozens or hundreds of result rows.

// Optimized: Clean split queries without row duplication
var orderDto = await db.Orders
    .AsNoTracking()
    .AsSplitQuery()
    .Where(o => o.Id == id)
    .Select(o => new OrderSummaryDto(
        o.Id,
        o.TotalAmount,
        o.Status,
        o.Items.Select(i => new OrderItemDto(i.ProductId, i.Quantity, i.UnitPrice)).ToList()
    ))
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync();

Benchmark Results

In our Tech Xpress catalog tests with 5,000 order history records, split queries and projection DTOs reduced data transfer from 4.8 MB down to 420 KB and reduced response time from 185 ms down to 24 ms.

title: Clean Architecture in .NET 8: Practical Separation vs Over-Engineering
snippet: How to apply Uncle Bob's Clean Architecture and CQRS without drowning in boilerplate interfaces and redundant mapping layers.
htmlContent:
Clean Architecture is frequently celebrated, yet frequently misunderstood. Developers often create 15 separate projects with redundant DTO-to-Domain-to-ViewModel mappers for a straightforward CRUD feature. Here is how I structure clean, pragmatic solutions.

The Four Core Tiers

  1. Core / Domain: Entities, Value Objects, and Domain Exceptions. Zero dependencies on ASP.NET Core, EF Core, or third-party packages.
  2. Application: Commands, Queries, Validators, and Interfaces. This layer declares what needs to happen using MediatR and FluentValidation.
  3. Infrastructure: Implementations of persistence, external payment gateways (Stripe), email providers, and system clock.
  4. API / Presentation: Controllers or Minimal API endpoints that map incoming HTTP requests into Application commands.

The Vertical Slice Compromise

Instead of spreading a single feature across 6 folders, group features into cohesive vertical slices within Application:

Features/
└── Invoices/
    ├── CreateInvoiceCommand.cs
    ├── CreateInvoiceValidator.cs
    ├── CreateInvoiceHandler.cs
    └── InvoiceCreatedEvent.cs

This allows rapid navigation, isolated unit testing, and confidence that modifications to invoice creation cannot unintentionally alter user authentication logic.

title: Mentoring Competitive Programming: Lessons from Graph Theory & Dynamic Programming
snippet: How coaching university students in ECPC contest preparation reinforces algorithmic rigor, edge case awareness, and O(1) performance thinking.
htmlContent:
At Port Said University's ECPC Competitive Programming Club, I had the privilege of coaching collegiate problem solvers in graph algorithms, data structures, and mathematical proofs. That experience transformed how I write software in production.

1. Big-O Complexity in Production

In contest environments, an O(N²) algorithm results in a Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) on test cases where N = 10⁵. In backend web development, the same mistake manifests as database timeouts and microservices crashing under traffic spikes. Understanding asymptotic limits enables engineers to instinctively choose hash maps O(1), balanced trees O(log N), or two-pointer sweeps O(N) before code hits staging.

2. Edge Case Paranoia

Competitive programming tests your code against hostile edge cases: integer overflow, empty collections, disconnected graphs, single-node trees, and boundary limits. In production, this mindset prevents null-reference exceptions, concurrency deadlocks, and silent financial calculation bugs.

3. Graph Theory in Real Software

Concepts taught in CP directly apply to enterprise software: dependency injection graphs are Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) resolved via Topological Sort; package dependency conflicts require cycle detection; and routing engines leverage Dijkstra and BFS.
